artifacts.author: GI Associates - Dr. R. Falk

Impression: Normal colonoscopy. Recommend routine screening interval per age-based guidelines (patient was then age 55).

artifacts.title: Primary Care Visit Note - Annual Exam
artifacts.author: Dr. A. Mensah, Internal Medicine
artifacts.body: 67-year-old woman presents for annual wellness visit. Reports chronic bilateral knee pain managed with OTC naproxen, using it regularly for several months. Denies chest pain, denies GI symptoms at that time. Cardiac: RRR, grade 2/6 systolic flow murmur at left sternal border, no radiation, no gallop. Abdomen soft, nontender. Plan: Continue current regimen, discussed weight-bearing exercise for knee OA, routine labs ordered for follow-up given fatigue complaints noted today.

facts.chart: 3 months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea on stairs
facts.says: I've just been so tired lately, and I get winded going up the stairs, which never used to happen.

facts.chart: Fatigue has gradually worsened over about 3 months
facts.says: It kind of crept up on me. A few months ago I'd just be a little tired by evening, now I'm dragging all day.

facts.chart: Dyspnea on exertion, specifically climbing stairs; denies dyspnea at rest
facts.says: Climbing the stairs to my bedroom leaves me huffing and puffing. I'm fine just sitting around though.

facts.chart: Denies chest pain, palpitations, or pressure
facts.says: No, nothing like chest pain or my heart racing, just the winded feeling.

facts.chart: Takes OTC naproxen 220 mg, two tablets twice daily for knee osteoarthritis, for about 8 months
facts.says: I take the naproxen from the drugstore, two pills in the morning and two at night, for my knees. Been doing that pretty regularly for maybe eight months now.

facts.chart: Chronic bilateral knee osteoarthritis, diagnosed several years ago, managed conservatively
facts.says: My knees have been bad for years, the doctor said it's just wear and tear arthritis.

facts.chart: Reports intermittent dark, tarry-appearing stools over past several weeks
facts.says: Now that you mention bathroom stuff... my stools have looked darker than usual sometimes, kind of black. I didn't think much of it, honestly it's a little embarrassing to talk about.

facts.chart: Denies bright red blood per rectum or on toilet paper
facts.says: No, I haven't seen any bright red blood, just that darker color sometimes.

facts.chart: Denies unintentional weight loss
facts.says: My weight's been about the same, I haven't been trying to lose anything or noticed clothes fitting different.

facts.chart: Reports a prior lab visit about 8 months ago where she was told her blood count was 'a little low' but did not follow up further
facts.says: Actually, now I remember, maybe eight months back my doctor mentioned my blood count was a touch low, but I felt fine then so I didn't think it needed more looking into.

facts.chart: Denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or heartburn
facts.says: My stomach doesn't hurt or anything, no burning, no throwing up.

facts.chart: Reports normal appetite, no early satiety
facts.says: I'm eating fine, same as always, no trouble finishing a meal.

facts.chart: Denies change in bowel habits, no diarrhea or constipation, no caliber change noted
facts.says: My bathroom habits are pretty regular otherwise, no diarrhea, no constipation that I've noticed.

facts.chart: No known family history of colorectal cancer; father had prostate cancer at age 78, mother had type 2 diabetes
facts.says: My dad had prostate cancer when he was real old, in his late seventies. My mom had the sugar diabetes. No colon cancer that I know of in the family.

facts.chart: Patient expresses embarrassment discussing bowel symptoms, delayed mentioning it
facts.says: I guess I was a little shy to bring up the bathroom stuff, it's not something you talk about easily.

facts.chart: Lives alone in a single-story home, widowed 5 years ago, has supportive adult daughter nearby
facts.says: I live by myself, my husband passed about five years back. My daughter checks in on me most days though.

facts.chart: Reports needing to rest midway up the stairs, has stopped her usual walking routine with a neighbor
facts.says: I used to walk with my neighbor every morning, but I've had to stop because I just can't keep up anymore. Sometimes I have to stop halfway up my own stairs.

facts.chart: Reports occasional lightheadedness on standing quickly
facts.says: A few times I've felt a little dizzy when I stand up fast from a chair.

facts.chart: Drinks alcohol rarely, less than one drink per month
facts.says: I almost never drink, maybe a small glass of wine at a holiday.

facts.chart: Never smoker
facts.says: I've never smoked a cigarette in my life.

facts.chart: No use of aspirin, anticoagulants, or prescription NSAIDs
facts.says: I don't take any blood thinners or aspirin or anything like that, just the naproxen and my multivitamin.

facts.chart: No prior history of peptic ulcer disease, GI bleed, or H. pylori infection
facts.says: I've never had an ulcer or any stomach bleeding before, as far as I know.

facts.chart: Reports a diet moderate in red meat and iron-containing foods, no recent dietary restriction
facts.says: I eat pretty normal, some meat a few times a week, vegetables, nothing special.

facts.chart: Postmenopausal since age 52, no vaginal bleeding
facts.says: Oh, I went through menopause years ago, no bleeding down there, that's long done with.

facts.chart: Prior cholecystectomy 15 years ago, no other major surgeries
facts.says: I had my gallbladder taken out a long time ago, that's really my only surgery.

facts.chart: Had a normal colonoscopy 12 years ago at age 55, has not had follow-up colonoscopy since
facts.says: I had one of those colon scope tests maybe twelve years back, they said everything looked fine, I guess I just never went back for another one.

facts.chart: Denies orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, or leg swelling
facts.says: I sleep fine lying flat, no swelling in my legs or anything like that.

facts.chart: Attributes fatigue to normal aging and tends to minimize symptoms
facts.says: I figured I'm just getting older, that's all, aches and tiredness come with the territory, right?

facts.chart: Wants to understand cause of fatigue and resume walking with neighbor
facts.says: I just want to know what's going on and get my energy back so I can walk with my neighbor again.

facts.chart: No known family history of anemia or bleeding disorders
facts.says: Nobody in my family that I know of has had anemia or bleeding problems.

facts.chart: Reports chronic bilateral knee pain and stiffness, worse with activity, unchanged in character recently
facts.says: My knees ache like they always do, nothing new there, that's just my arthritis.

facts.chart: Believes OTC naproxen is safe to use long-term since it is available without a prescription
facts.says: I didn't think it could be a problem since you can just buy it at the store without a prescription.

objectives.text: Elicit a history of chronic NSAID use and recognize its link to occult GI blood loss, including probing for embarrassing symptoms like melena
Correctly interpret CBC and iron study results to establish a microcytic, iron-deficiency anemia pattern distinct from anemia of chronic disease
Identify red-flag features requiring exclusion of colorectal malignancy despite a remote prior colonoscopy, and recommend appropriate referral/workup
Perform a feasible remote physical assessment for anemia (pallor, orthostatics) and correlate with functional impact

Recognize and address the mismatch between patient's recollection of being told blood counts were 'a little low' and the documented hemoglobin trend, demonstrating skill in exploring discrepancies with sensitivity

Formulate a management plan within medical student scope: stop/hold NSAID, arrange iron repletion workup, refer to gastroenterology for upper and lower endoscopy, and coordinate anemia follow-up with supervising physician

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient recalls being told about 8 months ago that her blood count was 'a little low' but believed it was minor and did not need follow-up
mismatches.recordEvidence: Hemoglobin trend chart shows Hb was already 11.4 g/dL (mildly low) 8 months ago, dropping further to 8.9 g/dL now, indicating a progressive, unaddressed anemia rather than a one-time minor finding
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may minimize or misremember the significance of previously flagged abnormal results; reviewing trends in the chart can reveal a pattern of worsening disease that was not acted upon, prompting better closed-loop follow-up systems.

patient.name: Helen Kowalczyk
patient.appearance: An older woman with gray hair pulled back, wearing a cardigan, seated at a kitchen table in a tidy home with soft overhead lighting. Her complexion appears somewhat pale on camera and she sits with slightly slumped posture, though her affect is pleasant and composed.

persona.personality: Stoic, polite, and a bit self-deprecating about her health complaints; tends to downplay symptoms as 'just getting older'
persona.communicationStyle: Speaks plainly and respectfully, gives direct answers once asked but does not volunteer embarrassing details unprompted; appreciates when the interviewer is warm and patient
persona.emotionalState: Mildly worried beneath a calm exterior, somewhat embarrassed about the bowel symptoms, relieved to finally have someone ask the right questions
persona.background: Worked as a school secretary for over 30 years before retiring, raised two children, widowed five years ago. Enjoys gardening, Polish cooking traditions with her daughter, and a daily walk with her neighbor that she has had to give up recently.
speechExamples: I don't like to make a fuss, but I suppose I have been feeling pretty worn out.
Oh, that's a bit personal, but I suppose you need to know.
I figured it was just my age catching up with me.
My daughter keeps telling me I should mention these things sooner.
concerns: Why am I so tired all the time?
Is this just part of getting older or is something actually wrong?
Will I be able to go back to walking with my neighbor?
Do I need to stop taking my arthritis medicine?

scenario.studentBrief: You are seeing Helen Kowalczyk, a 67-year-old retired school secretary, for a telehealth video visit. She booked the appointment for 3 months of worsening tiredness and shortness of breath climbing stairs. Recent outside labs are already in her chart. Take a focused history, perform the physical exam maneuvers feasible by video, review relevant results, and develop a differential diagnosis and initial management plan under your supervising physician.
scenario.chiefComplaint: Progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea for 3 months
scenario.openingLine: Hi, thanks for seeing me. I've just been feeling really worn out lately, and I get short of breath going up my stairs, which isn't like me at all.
tasks: Elicit a complete history of present illness including onset, progression, and associated symptoms
Perform feasible remote physical exam maneuvers
Review and interpret the laboratory results from the chart
Formulate a differential diagnosis and initial management plan

answerKey.primaryProblem: Iron-deficiency anemia due to chronic occult upper GI blood loss from long-term OTC NSAID (naproxen) use
differential: NSAID-induced gastritis/erosions with occult GI bleeding (most likely)
Colorectal malignancy or polyp causing lower GI blood loss (must be excluded given melena, anemia severity, and remote prior colonoscopy)
Anemia of chronic disease (less likely given clearly low ferritin and high TIBC)
Less likely: cardiac cause of dyspnea alone (exam and history not suggestive of heart failure)
keyFindings: Hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, MCV 72 fL, ferritin 6 ng/mL, elevated TIBC and RDW consistent with iron-deficiency anemia
Dark, tarry stools (melena) reported on direct questioning, patient initially embarrassed to disclose
Chronic high-dose OTC naproxen use for approximately 8 months without medical supervision
Hemoglobin trend shows progressive decline from 13.1 to 11.4 to 8.9 g/dL over 14 months, indicating an unaddressed, worsening process
Orthostatic hypotension (systolic BP drop of 22 mmHg) with compensatory tachycardia (HR rise of 22 bpm) and conjunctival pallor on exam supporting significant anemia
No prior colonoscopy follow-up in 12 years despite average screening interval recommendations
No alarm features for weight loss, but anemia severity and melena still warrant malignancy workup
plan: Advise patient to stop naproxen immediately and switch to acetaminophen or non-NSAID options for knee pain, discuss with supervising physician regarding alternative OA management
Send fecal immunochemical/occult blood test now, understanding this does not replace endoscopic evaluation

Refer urgently to gastroenterology for both upper endoscopy (to evaluate for NSAID-induced gastritis/ulcer) and colonoscopy (given 12-year interval since last exam and new anemia with melena) to exclude malignancy
Initiate oral iron replacement per supervising physician's guidance, with plan to recheck CBC and iron studies in 4-6 weeks
Educate patient on signs of worsening bleeding (worsening dark stools, dizziness, chest pain) and when to seek urgent/emergency care
Arrange close follow-up with supervising physician to review endoscopy results and adjust anemia treatment plan
Discuss safe use of OTC medications and the importance of reporting GI symptoms promptly in future
redFlags: Hemoglobin of 8.9 g/dL representing moderate-to-severe anemia with orthostatic hypotension, warranting prompt evaluation and likely same-week referral
Melena in the setting of chronic NSAID use raising concern for active or recent GI bleeding
12-year gap since last colonoscopy with new anemia and dark stools, requiring exclusion of colorectal malignancy regardless of absence of weight loss
Progressive, unaddressed hemoglobin decline over the past 14 months indicating a chronic ongoing process rather than an acute, self-limited event
educationPoints: Chronic NSAID use, even over-the-counter formulations, can cause significant upper GI mucosal injury and occult blood loss, especially in older adults
Microcytic anemia with low ferritin and high TIBC/transferrin saturation is a reliable pattern for true iron deficiency, distinguishing it from anemia of chronic disease
Patients may minimize or feel embarrassed about GI bleeding symptoms; using normalizing, direct language improves disclosure

Any patient with iron-deficiency anemia needs a source identified, and in postmenopausal women this almost always means GI evaluation at both ends regardless of a prior 'normal' colonoscopy if enough time has passed
Reviewing longitudinal lab trends in the chart can reveal clinically important patterns the patient may not recall or recognize as significant

Formal orthostatic hypotension is defined as a systolic BP drop ≥20 mmHg or diastolic drop ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing; smaller BP changes with only a heart rate rise represent a postural tachycardic response, not true orthostatic hypotension

profile.summary: A 67-year-old woman presents by telehealth with three months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnea, found to have severe iron-deficiency anemia on recent labs linked to chronic OTC naproxen use and previously unrecognized melena. The case teaches history-taking around embarrassing GI symptoms, interpretation of iron studies, and appropriate escalation for malignancy exclusion despite a reassuring but remote prior colonoscopy.
